relearning.title: Read: ionic bonds and naming
relearning.description: A short reading with the lunch-money analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can explain how ionic bonds form and name ionic compounds.**

**Think of lunch money.** If a friend hands you a dollar, the dollar moves from them to you: one gives and one takes. An **ionic bond** works the same way. A **metal** atom (the giver) **transfers** its valence electrons to a **nonmetal** atom (the taker).

**Step 1.** The metal **loses** its valence electrons and becomes a **positive ion**. Sodium (Group 1) loses 1 electron and becomes Na⁺.

**Step 2.** The nonmetal **gains** those electrons and becomes a **negative ion**. Chlorine has 7 valence electrons, gains 1 to reach 8, and becomes Cl⁻.

**Step 3.** **Opposite charges attract.** That attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ is the ionic bond.

Only electrons move. The protons never change. Both atoms end up with a full outer level, which makes them stable.

**The charges must cancel to zero.** Magnesium (Group 2) gives away 2 electrons, but each chlorine can take only 1. So one magnesium needs two chlorines: Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻ make **MgCl₂**.

**Worked example:** calcium and fluorine. Calcium has 2 valence electrons to give. Each fluorine takes 1. Calcium gives one electron to each of two fluorines: Ca²⁺ and two F⁻ make CaF₂.

checks.prompt: What happens to the electrons when sodium and chlorine form an ionic bond?

options.text: Sodium and chlorine share a pair of electrons
Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Chlorine transfers an electron to sodium

checks.explanation: Sodium is a metal, so it is the giver: it transfers its 1 valence electron to chlorine. That makes Na⁺ and Cl⁻, which attract. Saying the atoms share is the common mistake; sharing is a covalent bond.

checks.prompt: Oxygen needs 2 more electrons. Each potassium atom gives 1. How many potassium atoms does one oxygen atom need? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Each potassium gives only 1 electron, so it takes 2 potassium atoms to give oxygen the 2 it needs: K₂O. Using one of each (KO) is the common mistake.

sections.title: Formulas and names

body.text:
**Charges from the group number:** Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2, Group 13 = +3, Group 15 = −3, Group 16 = −2, Group 17 = −1.

**Writing the formula: crisscross applesauce.** Write each ion with its charge. Each charge drops to the bottom as the subscript on the **other** ion, with no sign. **Reduce** if you can, then **check** that the charges add to zero. The metal always goes first. Aluminum oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0.

**Naming.** Metal first, then the nonmetal with an **-ide** ending (chlorine → chloride, oxygen → oxide, sulfur → sulfide). **No prefixes, ever.** MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride, not magnesium dichloride.

**Polyatomic ions** keep their own name: NaNO₃ is sodium nitrate. In a formula they get parentheses only when you need 2 or more: Ca(NO₃)₂.

**Roman numerals.** Metals that can have more than one charge (transition metals like Fe and Cu, plus Pb and Sn) need a Roman numeral. It is the **charge**, not the number of atoms. Group 1, 2 and 13 metals never get one.

**Worked example:** Fe₂O₃. Three oxides are 3 × (−2) = −6. Two irons must total +6, so each iron is +3. Name: **iron(III) oxide**.

**Watch out for:** saying the atoms share electrons, prefixes on ionic names, using a subscript as the Roman numeral (Fe₂O₃ is not iron(II)), numerals on Group 1 or 2 metals, and putting -ide on a polyatomic ion (Na₂SO₄ is sodium sulfate, not sodium sulfide).

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of CaCl₂?
checks.explanation: Ionic names never use prefixes, and calcium (Group 2) has only one charge, so it gets no Roman numeral: calcium chloride. Adding di- because of the subscript 2 is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Chloride is Cl⁻. What is the correct name of CuCl₂?
checks.explanation: Two chlorides are −2, so the one copper must be +2: copper(II) chloride. Copper has more than one charge, so it needs the numeral. Using prefixes on an ionic compound is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why the formula for magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ and not MgCl. Say what the electrons do.

relearning.title: Do: flip the ionic rules, then build a bond step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then one compound worked from bond to formula to name.

cards.back: A metal transfers valence electrons to a nonmetal. The ions that form attract each other.
It loses electrons and becomes a positive ion. Na loses 1 and becomes Na⁺.
It gains electrons to reach 8 and becomes a negative ion. Cl gains 1 and becomes Cl⁻.
Opposite charges attract. The total charge of the compound is zero.
Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2, Group 13 = +3, Group 15 = −3, Group 16 = −2, Group 17 = −1.
Metal first, then the nonmetal ending in -ide. No prefixes. A Roman numeral only if the metal has more than one charge.

checks.prompt: In an ionic bond, what does the metal atom do?

options.text: It gains electrons and becomes a negative ion
It loses electrons and becomes a positive ion
It shares electrons with the nonmetal

checks.explanation: Metals are the givers: they lose their valence electrons and become positive ions. Saying the metal gains electrons is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Magnesium is in Group 2. Which ion does it form?
checks.explanation: Group 2 metals lose 2 electrons, so magnesium forms Mg²⁺. Metals make positive ions, so Mg²⁻ is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of Na₂O?
checks.explanation: Ionic names have no prefixes, and sodium (Group 1) never needs a Roman numeral: sodium oxide. Adding di- for the subscript 2 is the common mistake.

body.problem: Aluminum bonds with sulfur. Explain how the bond forms, then write the formula and the name.

steps.text: Who gives and who takes? Aluminum is a metal, so it gives. Sulfur is a nonmetal, so it takes. This is an ionic bond.
Find the ions. Aluminum (Group 13) loses 3 electrons: Al³⁺. Sulfur (Group 16) gains 2 electrons: S²⁻.
Make the charges cancel. Criss-cross: the 3 drops onto S and the 2 drops onto Al → Al₂S₃. Two aluminums give 6 electrons, and three sulfurs take 6.
Name it. Metal first, then the nonmetal with -ide. Aluminum has only one charge, so no Roman numeral: aluminum sulfide.

checks.prompt: Your turn: calcium is in Group 2 and nitrogen is in Group 15. Which ions do they form?
checks.explanation: Calcium is a metal and loses 2 electrons (Ca²⁺). Nitrogen is a nonmetal and gains 3 to reach 8 (N³⁻). Swapping the signs is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: what are the formula and name for the compound of calcium and nitrogen?
checks.explanation: Criss-cross Ca²⁺ and N³⁻: the 3 drops onto Ca and the 2 drops onto N → Ca₃N₂. Check: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0. Putting each charge on its own ion (Ca₂N₃) is the common mistake.

relearning.title: U3.LT2 Watch: ionic bonds and naming

checks.prompt: In an ionic bond, what happens to the electrons?

options.text: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal

checks.explanation: An ionic bond is like handing a friend a dollar: one gives and the other takes. The metal (the giver) transfers electrons to the nonmetal (the taker). Sharing is a covalent bond.

checks.prompt: Which pair of elements would form an ionic compound?
checks.explanation: Magnesium is a metal (left of the staircase) and oxygen is a nonmetal, so they form an ionic compound. Carbon + oxygen and nitrogen + hydrogen are two nonmetals (covalent). Calcium and magnesium are both metals, so they are not ionic.

sections.title: Naming ionic compounds with transition metals

checks.prompt: In the name iron(III) chloride, what does the Roman numeral III tell you?

options.text: Each iron ion has a +3 charge

checks.explanation: Like saying which size coffee you want, the Roman numeral is the size of the charge, not a count of atoms. Iron(III) means Fe³⁺. Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃, with only 1 iron.

checks.prompt: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the correct name of Fe₂O₃?
checks.explanation: Total negative: 3 × (−2) = −6. Two irons must total +6, so each is +6 ÷ 2 = +3. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Iron has more than one charge, so it needs the numeral: iron(III) oxide. Using the subscript 2 as the numeral is the common mistake, and ionic names never use prefixes.
